Purpose
pur'pus
n. (settled intention, design; rendering Hebrew etsah and chephets, Greek prothesis)
From the Old French porpos, from the Latin propono, to set before — a purpose is something set out in front and moved toward. Greek prothesis is built identically, pro and tithemi, a setting-before; it is also the word for the shewbread set before the LORD.

Biblical Definition

Purpose is settled intention, and Scripture uses it chiefly of God, whose purpose is the hidden spine of history. Paul's great consolation rests entirely on it: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28) — the working-together of all things is not a general optimism about the universe but a consequence of a purpose that governs it, and the promise is bounded by the calling. He states the scope of that purpose plainly: believers are “predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Ephesians 1:11). All things, not most things, and after the counsel of his own will, not in response to ours. Ecclesiastes sets the same truth in time: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Man's purpose is a smaller word but a real one, and Scripture commends it as resolve: Barnabas “exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord” (Acts 11:23). Divine purpose does not abolish human resolve; it is precisely what makes resolve worth having.

Webster 1828 Definition

Settled intention. God's purpose governs all things after the counsel of his own will and is the ground of Romans 8:28; man's purpose is real resolve, commended as cleaving to the Lord with purpose of heart.

expand to see more

PURPOSE, n. [Fr. propos; L. propono, to set before.] That which a person sets before himself as an object to be reached or accomplished; design; intention.

2. Intention; aim; end proposed; as, to what purpose is this waste?

3. Effect; consequence, good or bad; as, to little purpose.

4. Instance; example — an older use.

5. In Scripture, the eternal counsel of God; as, called according to his purpose, Rom. 8.

Key Scripture

Romans 8:28 — "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose."

Ephesians 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:"

Ecclesiastes 3:1 — "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:"

Acts 11:23 — "Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord."

Modern Corruption

Purpose has become a therapeutic project — the individual's search for personal meaning, discovered by looking inward. Scripture's purpose is God's, fixed before the foundation of the world, and the creature's peace lies in being caught up into it.

expand to see more

The self-actualising sense of purpose puts an unbearable weight on the individual, who must now generate significance out of his own preferences, and it fails exactly where it is most needed — in suffering, in obscurity, in old age, in a life that looks small. Romans 8:28 offers the opposite structure. The believer is not told to find his purpose; he is told he is called according to God's, and that this is why the wreckage works together for good. The comfort is external, and therefore available to a man who has run out of inner resources.

There is also a sub-Christian version that grants God a purpose but makes it responsive — God adjusting his plan to human decisions, which is the position open theism argues explicitly and which much popular preaching assumes without argument. Ephesians 1:11 shuts the door: he worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. The principle to recover is that a purpose which could be defeated could not comfort anyone. Precisely because God's purpose is unconditional, Barnabas's exhortation makes sense — cleave to the Lord with purpose of heart, since the One you cleave to will not be turned aside.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew etsah is counsel or plan and chephets is purpose fused with delight. Greek prothesis is a setting-before, used both of God's eternal purpose and of the shewbread; boule is deliberate counsel.

expand to see more

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, purpose, plan; the counsel of the LORD standeth for ever.

Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight and purpose together; the pleasure of the LORD that shall prosper.

Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting-before; God's eternal purpose, and the shewbread set before him.

Greek boule (G1012) — deliberate counsel, determinate will; joined to foreknowledge in Acts 2:23.

Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand, to predestinate; the verb tied to purpose in Ephesians 1:11.

Usage

"Of the ground on which all things work together for good: the called according to his purpose (Romans 8:28)."

"Of the scope of that purpose: him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Ephesians 1:11)."

"Of human resolve commended: with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord (Acts 11:23)."
